extracted.intended_audience: Calculus I instructors, mathematics-education researchers, and curriculum designers
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and implementing classroom tasks for undergraduate Calculus I that intentionally foster students' mathematical creativity (process-oriented, domain-specific). Includes task features, theoretical principles, implementation advice, and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of mathematical creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical creativity is defined as a process of offering new solutions or insights that are unexpected for the student with respect to their mathematics background or the problems they have seen before (process-oriented rather than product-oriented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus assessment and task design on students' processes (taking risks, making connections, conjecturing) rather than only final products. Distinguish creativity relative to the student versus creativity relative to the field; emphasize domain-specific creativity rather than domain-general creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gestalt principle (incubation/time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give students time to allow incubation to occur; tasks should be challenging enough to require incubation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement by assigning tasks to be worked on across time or outside class, revisiting tasks (call-back feature) as new material is introduced, and explicitly allowing time for thinking before requiring solutions. Juniper's practice of assigning work outside class and bringing it back is an example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic principle (value beauty/uniqueness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly value the beauty and uniqueness of solutions or methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When facilitating discussions or grading, praise novel/beautiful solutions and highlight unexpected insights. Encourage students to notice elegant approaches (e.g., valuing a novel factoring trick) and incorporate this valuation into classroom norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free-market principle (safe presentation/defense environment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a safe environment where students can present and defend their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure classroom norms so students can share partially-formed or risky ideas without penalty; use activities that invite multiple students to present varied approaches and encourage respectful critique and building on others' work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly principle (building off peers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow students to build off one another’s work; encourage scholarly interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitate whole-class or small-group discussions where students explicitly use, extend, or combine peers' ideas. Design tasks that make such building fruitful (e.g., multiple-solution tasks where one student's representation suggests another approach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty principle (tolerate ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolerate ambiguity and signal that it is acceptable to not immediately know a solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use open-ended or ill-defined prompts; reassure students that multiple solutions or interpretations are valid; avoid prematurely closing discussion. Jo’s instruction to students that 'there was not a single correct answer' exemplifies this practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-ended / ill-defined tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks that do not clearly define a single question or required approach, allowing many possible solutions and student-posed directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design prompts that invite problem posing and exploration (e.g., 'Is there anything in real life that is a perfect circle? How do you know?'). Such tasks promote conceptual discussion and student agency. Beware: explicit phrasing can reduce open-endedness (contrast 'find' vs 'is there...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-solution tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks that explicitly require students to solve a problem in different ways (different representations, properties, or cross-field properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to produce more than one approach (e.g., algebraic, graphical, numeric). Use prompts like 'Evaluate the limit in as many ways as possible.' Multiple-solution tasks foster originality, multiple representations, and deeper connections. They were the most frequently used feature by the instructors studied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks should allow and encourage different representations (algebraic, symbolic, graphical, verbal, gestures) of concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt students to translate between representations and compare insight gained. Design problems where different representations naturally suggest different solution paths (e.g., limit as slope of tangent vs algebraic manipulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem posing and student questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks should provide opportunities for students to pose problems and questions as part of the activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include prompts that invite students to generate examples, counterexamples, or follow-up questions. Encourage students to identify key research-like questions. This supports creativity and engagement with ill-defined problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote making connections between concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks should require or encourage students to connect different mathematical ideas and representations (relational understanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that cross topics (e.g., limits, derivatives, arc length) and prompt students to map relationships; use tasks that are unfamiliar/nonroutine to elicit creative mathematically-founded reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation / justification / proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks should ask students to evaluate mathematical statements and justify their reasoning (analysis of reasoning, justification skills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include prompts that explicitly require justification (e.g., 'Provide justification that the 2nd derivative test fails'); assess the quality of reasoning and the ability to critique or defend approaches as part of creativity-oriented assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjecturing, generalization, and example generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks should invite conjecture, generalization, and construction of examples or counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prompts that ask for generalization or ask students to construct instances illustrating a property. These activities support the development of creative, research-like mathematical thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / novelty and use of nonstandard tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks should allow for originality/novelty, including the use of tricks or less-standard algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and highlight unconventional but valid approaches; reward novelty in assessment and classroom discussion (aligns with the Aesthetic principle). Example: asking students to create a function meeting unusual constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incubation as an explicit feature
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing students time and opportunities to revisit problems so ideas can incubate and mature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use progressive reuse of a task across the semester (call-back feature), assign tasks as multi-day activities or homework followed by in-class discussion, and design PD or class structures that encourage delayed refinement of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid routinization in implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementation should not reduce the cognitive demand of tasks by over-specifying procedures or having teachers take over the challenging aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist specifying step-by-step procedures that strip ambiguity; scaffold without removing the inherently challenging elements; let students struggle productively rather than rushing to 'fix' or routinize tasks. Teachers should facilitate rather than monopolize problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation practices that support creativity-based tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete instructor actions to support task features and Sriraman’s principles (e.g., assure multiple solutions exist, allow presentation, provide incubation time, revisit tasks, assign as writing tasks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: explicitly tell students multiple solutions are acceptable; design tasks for progressive use across topics (call-back); have students write about open-ended tasks to practice mathematical communication; include opportunities for sharing and building on peers' work; provide ongoing PD and reflection on task design. Be mindful of assessment alignment (exams, reviews) so creativity-based tasks are valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment consideration for creativity-based tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment should account for processes (creativity, justification, multiple approaches) and not solely procedural correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rubrics or grading practices to reward originality, use of multiple representations, justification quality, and productive struggle. Note from the study: instructors discussed how to assess such work during PD, and one modified final-review materials to include non-routine creativity-based tasks.
